speaker: periodista
text: Good afternoon. Welcome to our press conference. I'm joined on stage by President Lagarde and Vice President Vujicic.

speaker: periodista
text: My name is Wolfgang Preussel. I also welcome the journalists who are following us online.

speaker: periodista
text: If they ask a question, I would ask them to turn on their cameras and put on their microphones.

speaker: periodista
text: And with that, I would like to hand over to President Lagarde, please.

speaker: presidenta
text: Well, thank you very much, Wolfgang, and good afternoon to all of you. The Vice President, our new Vice President, and I welcome you to our press conference.

speaker: presidenta
text: The Governing Council is committed to setting monetary policy to ensure that inflation stabilizes

speaker: presidenta
text: at our 2% target in the medium term.

speaker: presidenta
text: In line with this commitment, we today decided to raise the three key ECB interest rates

speaker: presidenta
text: by 25 basis points.

speaker: presidenta
text: The war in the Middle East is generating inflation pressures, and the decision to raise rates

speaker: presidenta
text: is robust across a range of scenarios, mapping out how the shock might evolve and affect

speaker: presidenta
text: the medium-term outlook for the euro area.

speaker: presidenta
text: In the baseline of the new euro system staff projections, headline inflation is expected

speaker: presidenta
text: to average 3% in 2016, 2.3% in 2017 and 2% in 2018.

speaker: presidenta
text: For inflation excluding energy and food, the baseline foresees an average of 2.5% in 2016

speaker: presidenta
text: Compared with March, staff have revised up their baseline projection for inflation in

speaker: presidenta
text: 26 and 27, owing to a higher path for energy prices, which to some extent is expected to

speaker: presidenta
text: feed into food, goods and services inflation.

speaker: presidenta
text: The baseline sees economic growth at an average of 0.8% in 26, 1.2% in 27 and 1.5% in 28.

speaker: presidenta
text: This is a downward revision for 26 and 27, reflecting a more pronounced impact of the

speaker: presidenta
text: war on commodity markets, real incomes and also confidence.

speaker: presidenta
text: The outlook remains uncertain, with upside risks for inflation and downside risks for

speaker: presidenta
text: economic growth.

speaker: presidenta
text: The full implication of the war for medium-term inflation and growth will depend on the intensity

speaker: presidenta
text: and duration of the energy price shock, as well as the scale of its indirect and second-round

speaker: presidenta
text: effects.

speaker: presidenta
text: This uncertainty is also reflected in the broad range of outcomes for inflation and growth

speaker: presidenta
text: in the updated illustrative scenarios put together by EuroSystem staff.

speaker: presidenta
text: These will be published with the staff projections on our website.

speaker: presidenta
text: With today's decision, we remain well positioned to navigate the uncertainty caused by the

speaker: presidenta
text: war.

speaker: presidenta
text: We will closely monitor the situation and follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting

speaker: presidenta
text: approach to determining the appropriate monetary policy stance.

speaker: presidenta
text: In particular, our interest rate decisions will be based on our assessment of inflation

speaker: presidenta
text: outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data,

speaker: presidenta
text: as well as the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are not pre-committing to a particular rate path.

speaker: presidenta
text: The decisions taken today are set out in a press release available on our website.

speaker: presidenta
text: So I will now outline in more detail how we see the economy and inflation developing,

speaker: presidenta
text: and will then explain our assessment of financial and monetary conditions.

speaker: presidenta
text: Let me first look at the economic activity.

speaker: presidenta
text: Adjusting for a temporary factor in Ireland, the euro-area economy grew in the first quarter, supported by domestic demand and exports. Yet the war in the Middle East is weighing on activity

speaker: presidenta
text: and surveys are pointing to a slowdown, especially in services. Manufacturing has held up so far.

speaker: presidenta
text: far. In part, this is because firms have been building up stocks to cope with supply chain

speaker: presidenta
text: pressures. It also reflects higher defense spending. The labor market remains resilient.

speaker: presidenta
text: Unemployment at 6.3% in April remains close to historical lows. The first quarter saw

speaker: presidenta
text: additional jobs being created, although at a slower pace than in the last quarter in 2025.

speaker: presidenta
text: Labour demand has cooled further, and firms and households expect the labour market to weaken.

speaker: presidenta
text: Looking ahead, staff now expect domestic demand to be weaker than they projected in March,

speaker: presidenta
text: as the war weighs on confidence and higher energy costs erode real incomes.

speaker: presidenta
text: At the same time, household balance sheets are solid overall, and consumption should remain the main driver of growth.

speaker: presidenta
text: Higher energy costs and lower confidence will dent private investment in the short run,

speaker: presidenta
text: but it should be underpinned by firms investing in new digital technologies.

speaker: presidenta
text: Even spending more on defence and infrastructure should continue to support public investments.

speaker: presidenta
text: These factors are expected to provide some cushioning against the fallout from the war.

speaker: presidenta
text: The Governing Council highlights the urgent need to strengthen the euro-area economy

speaker: presidenta
text: while maintaining sound public finances.

speaker: presidenta
text: Fiscal sustainability is a crucial anchor for broader economic stability.

speaker: presidenta
text: Fiscal responses to the energy price shock should be temporary, targeted and tailored,

speaker: presidenta
text: as emphasized in the European Commission 2026 European Semester Spring Package.

speaker: presidenta
text: Reforms to enhance the euro area's growth potential and accelerate the energy transition

speaker: presidenta
text: to reduce reliance on fossil fuels are more vital than ever.

speaker: presidenta
text: Completing the savings and investment union is key to funding innovation, supporting the

speaker: presidenta
text: green and digital transition, and improving productivity.

speaker: presidenta
text: The digital euro and tokenized wholesale central bank money will enhance Europe's strategic

speaker: presidenta
text: autonomy competitiveness and financial integration and will boost innovation in payments it is thus

speaker: presidenta
text: essential to swiftly adopt the regulation on the establishment of the digital euro

speaker: presidenta
text: simplifying and harmonizing rules across the eu single market will help european firms grow faster

speaker: presidenta
text: Let me now look at inflation. Inflation rose to 3.2% in May, from 3% in April.

speaker: presidenta
text: Energy price inflation ticked up to 10.9% in April, while food price inflation fell

speaker: presidenta
text: from 2.4% to 2%.

speaker: presidenta
text: Exclusion excluding energy and food picked up to 2.5% from 2.2% in April as goods inflation

speaker: presidenta
text: edged up to 0.9% and services inflation increased from 3% to 3.5%.

speaker: presidenta
text: Domestic cost pressures eased in the first quarter, supported by slower growth in wages

speaker: presidenta
text: and profits.

speaker: presidenta
text: ECB's wage tracker and surveys on wage expectations continue to indicate that wage growth should

speaker: presidenta
text: ease over the year. However, it is becoming more expensive for firms to source other inputs,

speaker: presidenta
text: and they therefore expect to put up their selling prices. Moreover, some indicators

speaker: presidenta
text: of underlying inflation have already been driven higher by the energy shock.

speaker: presidenta
text: Inflation expectations over shorter horizons remain well above levels before the outbreak

speaker: presidenta
text: of the war in the Middle East.

speaker: presidenta
text: At the same time, most measures of longer-term inflation expectations stand at around 2% supporting

speaker: presidenta
text: the stabilization of inflation around target in the medium term.

speaker: presidenta
text: The increase in energy prices will lift inflation further over the summer and keep it well above

speaker: presidenta
text: target into the first half of 2027.

speaker: presidenta
text: It will also have an impact on food, goods and services inflation.

speaker: presidenta
text: should then return to target in the second half of 27, supported by falling energy prices

speaker: presidenta
text: and slower increases in other prices.

speaker: presidenta
text: However, the war in the Middle East remains a major source of uncertainty, and the longer

speaker: presidenta
text: energy prices stay high, the more likely they are to drive up broader inflation through

speaker: presidenta
text: indirect and second-round effects. We will, therefore, closely monitor the size and persistence

speaker: presidenta
text: of the energy price increase and how it feeds through to price and wage setting, inflation

speaker: presidenta
text: expectations and overall economic dynamics. Turning now to the risk assessment. The risks

speaker: presidenta
text: to the growth outlook are to the downside, mainly owing to the war in the Middle East,

speaker: presidenta
text: which has added to the volatile global policy environment. Prolonged disruption of energy

speaker: presidenta
text: supplies could increase energy prices further and for longer than currently expected. These

speaker: presidenta
text: factors would erode real incomes even more and make firms and households more reluctant

speaker: presidenta
text: to invest and spend. The drag on growth would intensify if the closure of major shipping routes

speaker: presidenta
text: were to cause acute shortages of key inputs that forced euro-area firms to curtail output.

speaker: presidenta
text: A worsening of global financial market sentiment or a tighter supply of credit could dampen demand.

speaker: presidenta
text: Additional frictions in international trade could also further disrupt supply chain,

speaker: presidenta
text: reduce exports, and weaken consumption and investment.

speaker: presidenta
text: Other geopolitical tensions, in particular Russia's unjustified war against Ukraine,

speaker: presidenta
text: remain a major source of uncertainty.

speaker: presidenta
text: By contrast, growth could turn out to be higher

speaker: presidenta
text: if the economy and energy markets were to adapt more quickly than expected

speaker: presidenta
text: to the disruption caused by the war in the Middle East,

speaker: presidenta
text: or if the war was resolved promptly and sustainably.

speaker: presidenta
text: Moreover, planned defence and infrastructure spending reforms

speaker: presidenta
text: to enhance productivity and the euro area firms adopting new technologies

speaker: presidenta
text: may drive up growth by more than expected.

speaker: presidenta
text: A deeper integration of the single market would also boost growth

speaker: presidenta
text: beyond current expectations.

speaker: presidenta
text: The risks now to the inflation outlook are to the upside.

speaker: presidenta
text: If energy prices were to rise by more and for longer than currently expected,

speaker: presidenta
text: euro area inflation would increase further.

speaker: presidenta
text: This could be reinforced and become more persistent

speaker: presidenta
text: if higher energy prices were to spill over by more than expected to other prices and to wages,

speaker: presidenta
text: if longer-term inflation expectations were to rise in response,

speaker: presidenta
text: or if global supply chains were disrupted more broadly.

speaker: presidenta
text: Ongoing trade tensions could also give rise

speaker: presidenta
text: to more fragmented global supply chains,

speaker: presidenta
text: curtail the supply of critical raw materials,

speaker: presidenta
text: and worsen capacity constraints in the euro-area economy.

speaker: presidenta
text: Extreme weather events,

speaker: presidenta
text: and the unfolding climate and nature crisis more broadly,

speaker: presidenta
text: could drive up food prices by more than expected.

speaker: presidenta
text: By contrast, inflation could turn out to be somewhat lower if the economic effects of

speaker: presidenta
text: the war in the Middle East proved to be more short-lived than currently expected, or if

speaker: presidenta
text: indirect or second-round effects proved less pronounced than anticipated.

speaker: presidenta
text: volatile and risk-averse financial markets could weigh on demand and thereby lower inflation

speaker: presidenta
text: as well.

speaker: presidenta
text: So looking now at the financial and monetary conditions.

speaker: presidenta
text: Financial conditions are broadly unchanged since our last meeting, but remain tighter

speaker: presidenta
text: than before the war.

speaker: presidenta
text: The cost of issuing market-based debt rose to 4% in April from 3.9% in March.

speaker: presidenta
text: Bank lending rates for firms remained at 3.6% in April and mortgage rates at 3.4%.

speaker: presidenta
text: The annual growth rate of bank lending to firms increased to 3.4% in April from 3.2%

speaker: presidenta
text: in March, while the growth rate of corporate bond issuance rose to 4.6 percent.

speaker: presidenta
text: Mortgage lending in April again grew by 3 percent.

speaker: presidenta
text: In line with our monetary policy strategy, the Governing Council thoroughly assessed

speaker: presidenta
text: the links between monetary policy and financial stability.

speaker: presidenta
text: Euro-area banks are resilient, supported by strong capital and liquidity ratios, solid

speaker: presidenta
text: asset quality and robust profitability.

speaker: presidenta
text: However, a sudden sharp drop in asset prices, potentially amplified by the non-bank financial

speaker: presidenta
text: sector and deteriorating asset quality, particularly in energy and trade sensitive sectors, would

speaker: presidenta
text: pose risks to financial stability.

speaker: presidenta
text: These risks increase the longer the current geopolitical conflict lasts.

speaker: presidenta
text: Macroprudential policy remains the first line of defence against the build-up of financial

speaker: presidenta
text: vulnerabilities, enhancing resilience and preserving macroprudential space.

speaker: presidenta
text: So in conclusion, the Governing Council today decided to raise the three key ECB interest

speaker: presidenta
text: rates by 25 basis points.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are committed to setting monetary policy to ensure that inflation stabilises at our

speaker: presidenta
text: 2% target in the medium term.

speaker: presidenta
text: We will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary

speaker: presidenta
text: policy stance.

speaker: presidenta
text: Our interest rate decisions will be based on our assessment of the inflation outlook

speaker: presidenta
text: and the risks surrounding it in light of the incoming economic and financial data, as well

speaker: presidenta
text: as the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are not pre-committing to a particular rate path.

speaker: presidenta
text: In any case, we stand ready to adjust all of our instruments within our mandate to ensure

speaker: presidenta
text: that inflation stabilizes sustainably at our medium-term target and to preserve the smooth

speaker: presidenta
text: functioning of monetary policy transmission.

speaker: presidenta
text: And we now stand ready to take your questions.

speaker: periodista
text: First question today goes to Balazh Kaurani of Reuters, Balazh please.

speaker: vicepresidente
text: Good afternoon.

speaker: vicepresidente
text: First off, allow me to say a big hello to the newest member of the trio on stage, welcome

speaker: vicepresidente
text: Boris.

speaker: vicepresidente
text: President Lagarde, could you give us a flavor of the debate today?

speaker: vicepresidente
text: Were other options discussed perhaps a hold, perhaps a larger increase?

speaker: vicepresidente
text: the arguments put forth in the discussion. The second question is about your reaction function.

speaker: vicepresidente
text: I'm curious how much, how many more rate increases are embedded into the staff projections?

speaker: vicepresidente
text: What do you need to see to deliver on those? And will you have that sort of

speaker: vicepresidente
text: volume and quality of data available to you by July to make an informed decision?

speaker: presidenta
text: Thank you very much for your question and thank you for greeting the three of

speaker: presidenta
text: us and particularly Boris, our new Vice President. So the decision that we took

speaker: presidenta
text: today to raise by 25 basis points our three interest rates was a unanimous

speaker: presidenta
text: decision without reservation. We did not discuss, debate, any other alternative

speaker: presidenta
text: proposal and the one that was predicated on the euro system staff projections and

speaker: presidenta
text: the recommendations of our chief economist was unanimously endorsed. No

speaker: presidenta
text: discussion of others.

speaker: presidenta
text: Our reaction function has been very steady, repeated over the course of time,

speaker: presidenta
text: and I hope I will not offend you by repeating yet again that given the

speaker: presidenta
text: level of uncertainty that we are facing we will decide on a meeting by meeting

speaker: presidenta
text: basis we will be data dependent there will be no preset rate path in in our

speaker: presidenta
text: considerations and as a result of that it will be what it will be. Now this is

speaker: presidenta
text: not much by way of forward guidance but as you know under the present

speaker: presidenta
text: circumstances there is no such justification for the decision that we

speaker: presidenta
text: are making and that we will make in the future. I think I would add one thing

speaker: presidenta
text: Because I've read here and there that, oh, the ECB will make an insurance decision.

speaker: presidenta
text: It will be an insurance matter.

speaker: presidenta
text: It will be a preemptive rate decision.

speaker: presidenta
text: It's not at all the way we had our discussion, really.

speaker: presidenta
text: Our discussion were predicated on, obviously, the major energy shock that we have observed

speaker: presidenta
text: since the beginning of March that is enduring longer than what was expected by geopolitical experts

speaker: presidenta
text: and which we're beginning to see broadening throughout the economy with direct cost being

speaker: presidenta
text: obvious with indirect cost also showing up and as I said we will be monitoring attentively

speaker: presidenta
text: any further consequences of this major energy shock.

speaker: presidenta
text: Second response in relation to this insurance

speaker: presidenta
text: allegation of ours, which it was not.

speaker: presidenta
text: We have updated our scenarios,

speaker: presidenta
text: but if you remember from last time around,

speaker: presidenta
text: we had two scenarios which we published.

speaker: presidenta
text: We will be publishing a third scenario that will be available on our website,

speaker: presidenta
text: which we have decided to call the milder scenario.

speaker: presidenta
text: So, staff from the Euro system has worked on the update of the adverse and the severe scenarios,

speaker: presidenta
text: but they have also worked on a milder scenario in order to be on both sides of the baseline.

speaker: presidenta
text: And the decision that we took today to increase by 25 basis points all our interest rates

speaker: presidenta
text: is robust across the three scenarios.

speaker: presidenta
text: The two updated, adverse and severe, but also the milder scenario, which obviously is more

speaker: presidenta
text: positive and something that we should not neglect, but which is at this point in time

speaker: presidenta
text: unlikely to materialise. But we still thought that it was our duty to look at both sides.

speaker: presidenta
text: And on all accounts, our decision stands. And if we were not taking that very obvious

speaker: presidenta
text: monetary policy decision, then at the end of the medium term that we look out for projection

speaker: presidenta
text: purposes, we would be north of our target. So I hope I have covered your question.

speaker: periodista
text: Next question to Aneta Weisbach of CNBC. Aneta, please.

speaker: periodista
text: Thank you very much. Madame Lagarde, I have two questions, obviously. I would like to ask you

speaker: periodista
text: about the recent uptick in core inflation. We have seen that service prices are on the rise.

speaker: periodista
text: So is that, in your opinion, already a sign that we're seeing first signs of second round effects?

speaker: periodista
text: And then my second question would be, where are we in between all these scenarios?

speaker: periodista
text: Are we closer in the adverse camp? Are we approaching the severe camp?

speaker: periodista
text: What's the opinion of the ECB? Thank you very much.

speaker: presidenta
text: Well, on the services inflation, as you will have seen, it has moved from 3% to 3.5%,

speaker: presidenta
text: which is a significant increase.

speaker: presidenta
text: Now, obviously, what we need to understand better is what is under the skin of that increase

speaker: presidenta
text: and how we can distinguish between what is the direct and indirect consequence of the energy price's significant increase

speaker: presidenta
text: or whether there is something else.

speaker: presidenta
text: At this point in time, we cannot yet say whether this service price's significant increase

speaker: presidenta
text: is attributable exclusively to direct,

speaker: presidenta
text: to direct and indirect.

speaker: presidenta
text: What we are confident in, though,

speaker: presidenta
text: is that we are not seeing yet,

speaker: presidenta
text: we are not seeing yet second round effect

speaker: presidenta
text: which would be largely attributable to wages

speaker: presidenta
text: which play a significant contribution

speaker: presidenta
text: in the production of services.

speaker: presidenta
text: But I'm saying again

speaker: presidenta
text: that we will be monitoring closely

speaker: presidenta
text: closely all that in the months to come. Now you ask me where we stand, and I just want to take you back to a speech that I gave

speaker: presidenta
text: back in March, which I know you've been following, it was my speech to the ECB Watchers.

speaker: presidenta
text: And in March, at the ECB Watchers conference, I distinguished between three different situations,

speaker: presidenta
text: which are an analytical frame in and of itself, if you will.

speaker: presidenta
text: So I'm not going to consider that one is exactly scenario X, Y, or Z.

speaker: presidenta
text: But I said, first of all, if the shock is limited and short-lived,

speaker: presidenta
text: it's a case where we see through.

speaker: presidenta
text: Now, obviously, we do not find ourselves in this situation

speaker: presidenta
text: because we have decided and we think that it's a monetary policy

speaker: presidenta
text: that stands firmly on its own and that is robust across all scenarios, but we are not

speaker: presidenta
text: in that sort of let's see-through, it's going to be short-lived and small.

speaker: presidenta
text: The second situation that I referred to is the situation where the shock produces a large,

speaker: presidenta
text: though not too persistent, overshoot, in which case a measured adjustment of policy is needed.

speaker: presidenta
text: okay the third case that i referred to in that ecb watcher's speech is the situation where we expect inflation to deviate significantly and durably from target in which case the response

speaker: presidenta
text: must be appropriately forceful so i leave it to you to decide which of the three i've already

speaker: presidenta
text: eliminated case number one which is clearly not a situation where it's short-lived and and rather

speaker: presidenta
text: small. This is not the case. The decision we've made is not a forceful decision either, right?

speaker: presidenta
text: 25 basis points is a decision which clearly is a signal and is necessary given the economic

speaker: presidenta
text: situation that we have, given the uncertainty that we are navigating, given the inflation outlook

speaker: presidenta
text: that we have and the projections that have been produced by the Eurosystem staff.

speaker: periodista
text: Next question, Alex Weber of Bloomberg News. Alex, please.
Good afternoon. Thanks very much. On the sort of measured adjustment that you might be doing,
does the neutral range... That's what I said. You concluded that.

Does the neutral range play a role in your thinking in that regard? Is 2.5% for the deposit rate an important threshold? Or could a measured adjustment also mean a slight step into a restrictive territory?

And then secondly, so before today there were quite a few economists who've warned that a rate hike in the current environment would be a mistake. Did you reflect on these comments and what's your response to this?

speaker: presidenta
text: So, to the risk of disappointing you, we have not discussed the neutral rate, nor the range of neutral rate.

speaker: presidenta
text: As you know, there is a lot of work that has been done by staff in that respect, which

speaker: presidenta
text: have given a range within which the neutral rate would be located.

speaker: presidenta
text: Philip Lane has discussed that extensively in a speech recently, but we have not debated

speaker: presidenta
text: that our positioning with reference to the neutral rate, which I'll remind you is a bit

speaker: presidenta
text: bit difficult to actually assess precisely because we are not in a situation where there

speaker: presidenta
text: are no shocks, which is typically what you need to have as sort of an environment within

speaker: presidenta
text: which you determine where you are neutral because you don't stimulate, you don't restrict.

speaker: presidenta
text: So this was not debated at all by the governing council.

speaker: presidenta
text: So everybody has to do what they have to do.

speaker: presidenta
text: Our job is price stability.

speaker: presidenta
text: And our job is to apply the strategic review principles that we have agreed.

speaker: presidenta
text: Our job is to follow carefully the reaction function that you are all familiar with and

speaker: presidenta
text: that we try to be as transparent about as possible so that we are predictable.

speaker: presidenta
text: And in the face of that, frankly, given the numbers we have, given the inflation outlook,

speaker: presidenta
text: given the risk to the upside on inflation, given the robustness of the decision against

speaker: presidenta
text: and across all scenarios, the bad one, the very bad one, and the not-so-bad one, and

speaker: presidenta
text: the fact that it holds in all circumstances.

speaker: presidenta
text: And if you add to that the fact that our growth forecast as revised is 0.8%, you know, minus

speaker: presidenta
text: 0.1 relative to March, and 1.2 next year, and 1.5 the following year, it's not as if

speaker: presidenta
text: we are in an environment where growth is absent or under significant threat.

speaker: presidenta
text: A lot more can be done by structural reforms, by encouraging a European market that has no obstacles to trade, saving an investment union, and so on and so forth.

speaker: presidenta
text: And we encourage that very strongly in our monetary policy statement.

speaker: presidenta
text: Thank you.

speaker: periodista
text: Now, Ord Kersulek of BFM Business. Ord, please.
Thank you for taking my questions.
In the last meeting's minutes, some members mentioned the need for the ECB to avoid being perceived as complacent. Could you elaborate on this?
I wonder if today's decision is driven by communication or credibility purpose,
rather than by inflation expectation becoming unencured.
And secondly, your press release states that today's decision is robust across a range of scenarios.
Why use this word today, and does it mean that you have a clearer view of where weights are heading?

speaker: periodista
text: Thank you.

speaker: presidenta
text: Thank you very much for your two questions.

speaker: presidenta
text: One is, of course, we should not be complacent.

speaker: presidenta
text: I think that's a recurrent principle that we should always apply.

speaker: presidenta
text: as we should apply the principles of being data dependent,

speaker: presidenta
text: being analytical and rigorous about the analysis that we do of all the numbers that we receive.

speaker: presidenta
text: And this is what the Eurosystem staff has done

speaker: presidenta
text: and this is what will be done going forward by the ECB staff

speaker: presidenta
text: when they produce the next projections.

speaker: presidenta
text: So it's not an issue of complacency.

speaker: presidenta
text: And honestly, I don't like to brag and I'm not full of vanity, but I would hasten to add that having maintained inflation

speaker: presidenta
text: pretty much at target over the last 12 months,

speaker: presidenta
text: we have not been complacent.

speaker: presidenta
text: We have done our job and we will continue doing so.

speaker: presidenta
text: So on your second question,

speaker: presidenta
text: the characterization of robustness of the decision is obviously

speaker: presidenta
text: helpful when you do scenarios across the board. So if we had done, you know, severe and adverse

speaker: presidenta
text: scenario, sorry, adverse and severe scenario, and then decided it was robust, yeah, of course it is

speaker: presidenta
text: robust. But we decided on purpose to do scenarios on both sides of the baseline. And even in

speaker: presidenta
text: the milder scenario, the 25 basis points cuts is completely warranted and justified. So

speaker: presidenta
text: this is what we've done.

speaker: periodista
text: And now Olaf Storbeck of the Financial Times. Olaf, please.
Hi, I have one question on the inflation forecast. What struck my eye when I compared the current
baseline with a March adverse scenario, the headline inflation is lower than in the adverse
scenario, but the core inflation is higher for 26. Does this mean that kind of spillover effects
are already bigger than you anticipated in March and what are driving them? And my second question
is you clearly said this rate hike isn't an insurance hike what is it then is it the start
of a new hiking cycle or or what else thanks well thank you very much for your two questions

speaker: presidenta
text: so on with reference to the baseline first of all i i have not compared and we have not gone

speaker: presidenta
text: into the exercise of comparing the baseline

speaker: presidenta
text: with the adverse or the severe scenario

speaker: presidenta
text: at this point in time.

speaker: presidenta
text: We have updated our baseline

speaker: presidenta
text: both on the account of inflation

speaker: presidenta
text: and on the account of growth as well.

speaker: presidenta
text: With the caveat of Ireland,

speaker: presidenta
text: which is a case in point

speaker: presidenta
text: of international companies

speaker: presidenta
text: organizing their business in such a way

speaker: presidenta
text: that it impacts

speaker: presidenta
text: in an interesting way

speaker: presidenta
text: the Irish numbers.

speaker: presidenta
text: So what we have done

speaker: presidenta
text: is that we've updated the baseline.

speaker: presidenta
text: And I think the best thing that can be done

speaker: presidenta
text: is to compare the adverse scenario prepared in March

speaker: presidenta
text: with the adverse scenario compared with June.

speaker: presidenta
text: I think that is more relevant than baseline

speaker: presidenta
text: versus last time around adverse.

speaker: presidenta
text: And as I told you in the earlier phase

speaker: presidenta
text: of our discussions today,

speaker: presidenta
text: we are beginning to see a broadening

speaker: presidenta
text: of inflation throughout the economy.

speaker: presidenta
text: And that is obviously in terms of direct effect,

speaker: presidenta
text: but also in terms of indirect effect.

speaker: presidenta
text: Not yet at this point in the front of the second round effect.

speaker: presidenta
text: But we are going to be extremely attentive.

speaker: presidenta
text: And when we see, for instance, that the delivery dates,

speaker: presidenta
text: that the smoothness of supply is beginning to be impaired,

speaker: presidenta
text: obviously we will be attentive to those sort

speaker: presidenta
text: of auxiliary indicators that would help us understand

speaker: presidenta
text: where it is heading.

speaker: presidenta
text: One more point, because I did speak about wages earlier.

speaker: presidenta
text: We do include a level of second round effect

speaker: presidenta
text: in our projections, obviously.

speaker: presidenta
text: And the projections that we have for both, for the three years, actually, 26, 27, 28,

speaker: presidenta
text: all anticipate compensation per employee at 3.2%.

speaker: presidenta
text: Which, in and of itself, if you compare that with the projections that we have on inflation,

speaker: presidenta
text: justifies the fact that the net income of workers will actually be positive.

speaker: presidenta
text: And would lead to assume that consumption will continue,

speaker: presidenta
text: not only will continue to be the main driver of growth, as it is,

speaker: presidenta
text: but will continue to grow probably more than other factors.

speaker: presidenta
text: We see other factors to fuel growth going forward.

speaker: presidenta
text: Now, yes, I did say that it's not an insurance policy interest rates decision,

speaker: presidenta
text: simply because it's a good monetary policy interest rate decision.

speaker: presidenta
text: When you have the latest reading at 3.2, When you have the inflation outlook over our target, peaking in the end of 26, continuing to be over target throughout most of 27, returning to 2% in the autumn of 27, and being at target in 28, on the basis of market curves and all the rest of it,

speaker: presidenta
text: it is pretty obvious that we have to make a decision,

speaker: presidenta
text: that it is a sensible monetary policy decision.

speaker: presidenta
text: So I don't need to characterize it as credibility, insurance,

speaker: presidenta
text: or anything else, for that matter.

speaker: presidenta
text: It's a monetary policy decision that stands,

speaker: presidenta
text: and that is, as we say in the monetary policy statement,

speaker: presidenta
text: robust across all scenarios, including the mild one.

speaker: periodista
text: Moving to the other side of the room, Nina Ninkovic.

speaker: periodista

Ah, welcome.
Thank you.
Hello, I have a question for Madame Lagarde.
Croatia is one of the newest members of the Eurozone,

Thank you.

speaker: presidenta
text: Well, thank you very much to your question. We are, of course, delighted that Croatia is a member of the Euro area, and I and all

speaker: presidenta
text: governing council members and members of the executive board are delighted to have the

speaker: presidenta
text: Croatia National Bank, I was going to say former governor, being now a member of the

speaker: presidenta
text: executive board and the new vice president of the ECB.

speaker: presidenta
text: It's a great representation and it brings diversity amongst the group and it's really

speaker: presidenta
text: a blessing that Boris has joined us.

speaker: presidenta
text: But turning to inflation, of course we're concerned about inflation, but we are not

speaker: presidenta
text: just concerned about inflation in one member state or the other because our job at the

speaker: presidenta
text: ECB is to look at the whole of the euro area.

speaker: presidenta
text: And our concern, as I said earlier on, is that we see the energy price inflation, you

speaker: presidenta
text: know, 10.9% at the moment, broadening throughout the economy, which is why we are making this

speaker: presidenta
text: decision today.

speaker: presidenta
text: Broadening inflation outlook, underlying inflation, all of that point in the direction of having

speaker: presidenta
text: to make a decision of increasing interest rates.

speaker: presidenta
text: So because our mission, our mandate, is to restore price stability, we make those decisions.

speaker: presidenta
text: And we are driven by that objective, price stability.

speaker: presidenta
text: Thank you.

speaker: periodista
text: Next question goes to Klaus-Reiner Jakisch of the German broadcaster HR.
Good afternoon.
Mrs. President, given some of the statements of members of the governing council previous
to this meeting, one could have expected that the projections for inflation is much higher.

And the second question, as you know, there's already a lot of criticism despite this very
moderate rate hike, especially by the unions who fear that growth could be dampened even
further.
What do you say to them?
Thank you very much.

speaker: presidenta
text: Well, thank you very much.

speaker: presidenta
text: As I said, our mission, our mandate is price stability.

speaker: presidenta
text: We have defined price stability for our strategy review and our purpose of making decisions

speaker: presidenta
text: at 2% in the medium term.

speaker: presidenta
text: you see inflation picking up in the way it does, broadening throughout the economy, when

speaker: presidenta
text: you see inflation outlook north of that 2% target and only returning to 2% at the end

speaker: presidenta
text: of our projection horizon, when you see risk to the upside, to us, this is inflation that

speaker: presidenta
text: needs to be taken into account and that needs to be addressed.

speaker: presidenta
text: I don't know what other governors in whatever publication or interviews you refer to

speaker: presidenta
text: allege that it would be higher inflation.

speaker: presidenta
text: But we do have inflation that is too high for our citizens,

speaker: presidenta
text: that is too high for the purpose of price stability as well.

speaker: presidenta
text: And we will address that because our commitment is price stability.

speaker: presidenta
text: your second question was about the risk

speaker: presidenta
text: resulting from this decision

speaker: presidenta
text: first of all I would observe that

speaker: presidenta
text: the main risk

speaker: presidenta
text: would be not to take that kind of

speaker: presidenta
text: decision because if you

speaker: presidenta
text: let inflation start

speaker: presidenta
text: running out without control

speaker: presidenta
text: then it becomes a much

speaker: presidenta
text: more difficult situation to bring it

speaker: presidenta
text: back to the level of price

speaker: presidenta
text: stability that we have defined

speaker: presidenta
text: So the good decision was actually to raise interest rates, to commit and to deliver on price stability so that people will make their investment decision, their employment decision, their wage negotiations decisions in the light of that commitment to restore price stability as we will.
And now Elisa Piazza of CLAS, CNBC, Italian Broadcaster. Thank you for taking my question.
Well, you do not say anymore in your statement that longer term inflation expectations remain
well anchored.
So if you could tell us a little bit more about this change.
And then I have another question on another topic, because we know that the ECB has convened
banks to discuss the risks associated with the new AI models such as Mythos. So what actions is
the ECB taking on this issue and do you consider these models to pose a potential systemic risk
to the European banking sector? Thank you. Thank you so much for your two questions. So

speaker: presidenta
text: in terms of inflation expectations, we'll look at three categories of expectations.

speaker: presidenta
text: We look at market-based measures, we look at survey-based measures, and we look at consumers' expectations.

speaker: presidenta
text: And we try to understand exactly where those expectations stand between the short-term and the medium-term that is relevant for our monetary policy decisions. And what we see at the moment is short-term inflation expectations that have risen in all three categories, more so from the consumers because that is typically the case.

speaker: presidenta
text: But when you look at the longer-term expectations, they are broadly anchored at our 2%.

speaker: presidenta
text: And whether you look at, you know, one in one, five in five, one in five, you have the whole category of intervals to look at.

speaker: presidenta
text: And on all those accounts, inflation expectations are broadly anchored.

speaker: presidenta
text: So you asked me about the, I will call it artificial intelligence at large.

speaker: presidenta
text: but it's clearly the most recent development of artificial intelligence,

speaker: presidenta
text: whether it's by Anthropic or by OpenAI

speaker: presidenta
text: or by other major developers and investors in artificial intelligence

speaker: presidenta
text: or whether it's from other countries.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are seeing significantly new, faster, more intrusive developments.

speaker: presidenta
text: That is a fact.

speaker: presidenta
text: We also know that these developments are here to stay and that they will continue to be more in the coming months

speaker: presidenta
text: and probably on an ongoing basis.

speaker: presidenta
text: So that calls for two categories of responses.

speaker: presidenta
text: One that addresses our own central bank.

speaker: presidenta
text: Are we at the ECB and other national central banks

speaker: presidenta
text: around in the euro system well-equipped

speaker: presidenta
text: to actually resist potential intrusion, potential hacking,

speaker: presidenta
text: potential negative intrusion that would be using those tools.

speaker: presidenta
text: And this is work that is underway,

speaker: presidenta
text: and this is one that we take very seriously

speaker: presidenta
text: because obviously we are a central part of the financial world.

speaker: presidenta
text: The second, which is more under the limit of the SSM,

speaker: presidenta
text: has to do with how we help, flag, call the attention of all the banks that we supervise to make sure that they too, and I know that they do, but that they too pay particular

speaker: presidenta
text: attention in order to protect themselves and make sure that possible intrusion that operate

speaker: presidenta
text: at a fast pace are not going to hurt them.

speaker: presidenta
text: So I think everybody is looking at this very carefully.

speaker: presidenta
text: We do not all have access to the latest tools of some of those developers that I have mentioned. But there are ways, not necessarily using the ultimate state-of-the-art and latest version,

speaker: presidenta
text: but there are ways to actually protect ourselves, do the necessary patching,

speaker: presidenta
text: and make sure that we are as secure as possible.

speaker: presidenta
text: So all of that is taking place.

speaker: presidenta
text: So that's one category.

speaker: presidenta
text: I think there is another category that is, you know, worth discussing,

speaker: presidenta
text: which has to do with how governments, how sovereigns,

speaker: presidenta
text: actually respond to these risks,

speaker: presidenta
text: of which I think we are seeing maybe the top of the iceberg,

speaker: presidenta
text: and for which more significant risk should be anticipated,

speaker: presidenta
text: and possibly joint framework, joint governance should be discussed at a higher level. But for the moment, at our limited level, as a central bank,

speaker: presidenta
text: we do what we can in response to these developments that are here to stay.

speaker: presidenta
text: Thank you.
